Question: Do Facebook software engineers get paid less than software engineers at other companies like Microsoft, Amazon and Google? If so, why is this the case?
Answer: This is highly dependent on how the stock is doing. That’s the stock of these companies over the last 5 years. Let’s suppose that you get a job offer with either of them in 2018. They offer you 200k a year and 1m in stock over 4 years. Actually let’s pretend the stock vests over 5 years to make this chart more relevant. Let’s also pretend you never get raises or bonuses or equity refresh just to make our maths simpler and that you never sell your stock until it vests in full. So 5 years later: With Google, you’ll have received 3,194,700 over 5 years. (5 * 200000 + 1m * (1 + 119.47%)) With Amazon: 2,256,900. With Microsoft: 3,729,800. With Meta: 2,805,100. So there’s a difference of 65% between Microsoft and Amazon. Candidates have 0 clue how the stock of their companies will evolve over the next 5 years. To make things more complicated, they grow at a different pace. There are definitely been periods where each of these companies offered the highest compensation. Over the past year, Meta stock has been growing much faster than any of the other 3 (which you can see at the end of the graph).

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Is learning Git necessary for any beginner programmers who want to work in web development?
Answer: I don’t think so, it is arguably the most common source control tool today but there are lots of organizations that do not use it. Also, it’s technically possible to do web development without source control. Understanding how source control work is certainly useful, but for instance it can be argued that understanding databases and/or SQL is also useful given how ubiquitous databases are in software development, and yet I wouldn’t say that it is necessary to become a web developer. Same goes for git.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: How likely is it that Google's laid-off employees will be able to find open positions elsewhere within the company?
Answer: Very unlikely. Pre 2023 layoffs, Alphabet had roughly 190000 employees. They cut 12000, to ~178000. So to the 12000 that were laid off, let’s add 10% of natural attrition (Alphabet is supposed to be a little less than that but let’s give them 10%). Let’s round up to 18000, and say that employees that left Alphabet willingly or not since the last layoff round is 30000. That gives us 160000 employees who started before January 2023. Pre 2024 layoffs, Alphabet had 182000 employees. So, over 2023–2024, Alphabet would have hired 22000 people. If that seems like a lot, we can remove former interns and other new grad hires (let’s say 3000) - any one who’s worked is not going to be able to enter the company through these channels. Alphabet didn’t increase its employee count much through acquisitions in 2023 (less than 100 people) so we can ignore that. So we have 19000 people hired by Google over last year. If applications have gone at the same pace as before, which is likely, then that’s 3000000 per year. That means that 0.06% of applicants will get a job. If all people who were laid off were to apply, statistically less than 1 would be re-hired. Traditionally former google employees had an advantage when applying but I don’t think that’s the case of laid off employees.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Do employers prioritize hiring software engineers who can code quickly over those who take their time to write accurate and efficient programs?
Answer: Those two things are not contradictory. Professional software engineers write good clean code fast. There is no guarantee that taking more time for the sake of taking more time is going to result in better code. However, code must pass certain quality requirements in order to be committed to the code base. So these professionals are neither slow nor sloppy.
